segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You may remember this story that we did about a year ago, about canvassers going door to door and talking to voters for 20 minutes. And in just 20 minutes, the canvassers got some voters to change their minds, to flip positions on big, hot button issues. Gay marriage. Abortion.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Which, of course, is amazing, right? That is not something that seems like it's even possible. There was a study in a well-known, peer reviewed journal-- Science magazine-- proving how remarkably effective these people were. They invented a whole new way to sway voter opinion. It seemed like a game changer, a whole new tool for politics, for liberals or conservatives to use.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then a month after our radio story-- maybe you saw this in the news-- there was overwhelming evidence that one of the researchers, a grad student named Michael LaCour had fabricated all the data. Science magazine retracted the article.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But the team that invented this canvassing technique, they were not the ones that did the research study. That was a separate thing. And they were just as shocked as anybody. Maybe more shocked.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The week the news broke, one of the canvass organizers, Steve DeLine, told me they'd spent months meticulously going door to door and keeping perfect records of everything they were doing for this researcher. To find out that LaCour had just made up his part of the data--

segments.speaker: Steve Deline
segments.text: It's unfathomable to me, having you know, made sure that we were dotting every I and crossing every T. And you know, jumping through every hoop that he asked of us. It's just-- just can't really explain it. I'm at a loss.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Then in August, three months after the retraction, four months after our story aired--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Hi.

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: Hi.

segments.speaker: Steve Deline
segments.text: Steve.

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: Dave.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Hi.

segments.speaker: Steve Deline
segments.text: Nice to meet you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Nice to meet you guys in person.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We got a visitor to our office from two of the guys who'd developed this canvassing technique, that guy Steve and his coworker Dave Fleischer. They happened to be in town from California. And they had news.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A brand new study with new researchers was looking into their work. Results were coming in. Here's Dave.

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: We're not anticipating going public with these results until January at the earliest, and maybe not till June.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What these researchers really wanted to do was publish their results in Science magazine, you know, the place that published the original, discredited study. In fact, one of the researchers was laying the groundwork for that.

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: So he actually called up Marcia McNutt, who's the editor of Science. And they didn't immediately reject it out of hand. She just said, "You know, the bar's going to be very high." [LAUGHS] Well, no [BEEP] fooling.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, apparently Science magazine liked what the new researchers did. This week they published the new study about these canvassers.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This one's not fake. We know now, for real, whether those canvassers are, in fact, convincing anyone of anything when they go door to door. And if anything, what the canvassers are achieving and the way that they're achieving it is even more interesting than the fake study said.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago and This American Life, I'm Ira Glass. Today on our program, "For Your Reconsideration." We have this story and two other stories where people go back and revisit evidence from the past. And just to start this off, in case you didn't hear our first story about those canvassers a year ago, here's what they were. If you heard that show, this will just be a quick reminder.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: Hi. We're talking to registered voters in your neighborhood today about their views on abortion.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is one of the canvassers. She's young, with tattoos and a halter top. It's a warm Los Angeles day, and the voter's on the other side of a screen door. She's older, heavyset, wire rimmed glasses. She's a nurse.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And OK, just to be clear, what you're about to hear is a real canvasser with a real voter. This is not part of the discredited study. This is from a video of one of the regular canvasses these guys Dave and Steve organized. The canvasser begins by asking this voter what she believes about abortion on a scale from zero to 10.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: Zero means you think women should have no access to abortion. 10 means women should have full access to abortion.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The voter says zero. No access. No abortions for anybody. She's Catholic, from Mexico.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And they start talking about how hard it can be to discuss abortion. Even with family.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: How did that feel for you to talk to your daughters?

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: It's not easy. It's not easy, because in my country they have taboos, a lot of taboos. And my mother is one of the person never talking about sexual relations or conceptions.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: That's why I try to be very open with my daughters.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Notice that this conversation's just begun and already she's talking about her daughters and her mom. That's no accident. This whole technique is built around having a very personal conversation, a very real conversation about the voter's experiences. To make that happen, this canvasser does something that a lot of the canvassers do-- she talks about her own experiences.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: My mother's from the Philippines.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: And my mother went through the same thing. Like, it's not something that you talk about.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: No. It's not.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: Huh.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: In my family, it's the same.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: When I got my period, I was 12 years old.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: And--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The voter tells her that when she was 11 and got her period, nobody explained what was happening. She thought she was dying.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: And I believe I am dying. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: Oh! [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And when she was six, her mom miscarried a baby. But nobody explained what was going on to her. And so she's tried to be different with her daughters and talk to them. That's why she became a nurse, she says, to help women.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So these two strangers are swapping stories and really talking from the heart. And 15 minutes into this 22-minute conversation, the canvasser circles back to the subject at hand in a very pointed way.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: I had an abortion.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: In November this past year.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: Oh, I'm so sorry.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: And it wasn't the wrong choice for me.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: Because that's what felt right for me. But I was alone.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: And it was scary.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: And it wasn't-- it was because I don't know how to talk about it with people. Like, my family, my mother loves me. And so does my papa and my sister.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: But--

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: I know, but it's hard. And you carry it for the rest of your life. It's your decision--

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: But you carry it for the rest of your life.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: If you are-- one of the things that I struggled with with telling my family is this idea that my family's going to love me less.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: No. Never.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: Would you ever love your daughters less?

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: No. Never.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's a moment that's simultaneously intimate and manipulative and honest all at once. And it works.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: After this, the canvasser asks the voter again to rate on a scale of zero to 10 where she stands on access to abortion. Remember, she was a zero before.

segments.speaker: Canvasser
segments.text: We have that same zero to 10 scale where zero means no access and 10 means full access.

segments.speaker: Female Voter
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She's been standing at the door just 18 minutes. So again, OK, that's real. That is not part of the fraudulent study.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The team that invented this technique of going door to door-- including Dave Fleischer and Steve Deline, the two guys who visited our office at the beginning of this story-- they work at the Los Angeles LGBT Center, which is a big, multimillion-dollar nonprofit, the biggest LGBT organization in the world. They started doing these canvasses in 2009. They were hoping to change voters' minds to support gay marriage. This was in the wake of Proposition 8, which rejected gay marriage in California.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And they discovered through trial and error that the trick to this whole thing was they don't try to reason with people about rights and equality and big principles like that. Canvass organizer Steve Deline says if you're talking at a kind of rational, sort of intellectual level about things, you're gonna fail.

segments.speaker: Steve Deline
segments.text: That's not where people make their decisions about issues like this. People make their decisions about how they're going to vote on this at a gut level and at a visceral level and an emotional level.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is what they learned-- to stop telling people things. The most important thing the canvasser should do is listen.

segments.speaker: Steve Deline
segments.text: I think the big revelation was that our job was actually to go and give them the chance to talk about their own life, and realize that you know, maybe that led them to conclusions that were a little different than they'd thought.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So they're out doing this, trying their canvasses. And it took them less than a year to start to get decent results like you heard with that nurse. A small but noticeable number of people at the door told them that their minds had been changed.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But of course, the only way to tell for sure if their minds changed and stayed changed was to have outsiders-- scientists-- do a proper case control study. And that's why the canvassers invited in two political scientists to do the original study that was published in Science magazine. That grad student from UCLA-- Michael LaCour-- did the actual research. But the study design and results were overseen by a big deal political scientist from Columbia University named Donald Green, who's kind of legendary in that world for transforming how people do field experiments. And Green says that before they started, he expected the results were going to show--

segments.speaker: Donald Green
segments.text: Short-term effects. I thought that those effects would subside in a few days' time.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He thought that 'cause pretty much that's what always happens. People change their minds and then the effect wears off. Or much more common, they don't change their minds at all.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's a hefty body of research documenting something called the backfire effect, which happens with most of us. When we're confronted with evidence disproving something that we personally believe, most of us generally just dig in, and we believe it more.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is a phenomenon, by the way, that's familiar to anybody who's ever been to a Thanksgiving dinner during an election year and tried to argue with some favorite uncle's wrongheaded political opinions. Never works, right? Facts mean nothing. And by the way, Uncle Lenny, I am not talking about you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But this is what was so revolutionary about the data that this grad student seemed to be gathering about these canvassers. He said he did online surveys with the voters who got visited by the canvassers and they showed that their minds changed and stayed changed for six months, nine months, a year after the canvasser knocked at the door.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Green told me that he and his colleagues had read through over 900 papers, never seen anything like this result, to change people's opinions and have it last like this. Though interestingly, when LaCour first showed his data to Professor Green, Green thought, this data is so perfect, these results might be real. But OK, best to be sure.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And he told LaCour to do the entire study-- canvasses, surveys, everything-- a second time. Which LaCour did. Same result.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, of course, later, Green's suspicions would be confirmed in spades. All that data would be shown to be fraudulent. But here's what LaCour said he found in the original study published in Science .

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so what I'm about to say is from the discredited results of a retracted study. This study was about gay marriage. It was about convincing people to support gay marriage. And the study claimed that a year after the canvassers visited voters' homes, the number of voters supporting gay marriage had jumped 15%. 15%.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But-- and this was key-- according to the study, the 15% increase only happened if the canvasser at the door had been gay and admitted being gay to the voter. People who talked to other canvassers only rose 3%, which is about as much as the nation as a whole changed on the issue of gay marriage that year.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It was a similar effect with abortion, according LaCour. He said the number of people who became pro-choice after the canvass rose 5%. And again, the effect only lasted if the canvasser at the door revealed that she had had an abortion. It was talking to somebody affected by the issue that seemed to be changing people's minds.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I actually interviewed Michael LaCour a year ago for the story that I did for our show about all this. I have to say, it's strange listening to that interview today, knowing what happened just a few weeks after we talked, that his data would be shown to be fraudulent. 'Cause when I talked to him, he really talked like somebody doing a real study with real surveys. Like for instance, I asked him how attitudes towards abortion changed over time among the voters that he was studying.

segments.speaker: Michael Lacour
segments.text: So that's still ongoing. Because I'm tracking longitudinally these individuals over a course. I don't want to give out a hard number, but it stays relatively flat. And I think it levels off around five percentage points. That's around 200 days later.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He offered conclusions from his data. Like this one.

segments.speaker: Michael Lacour
segments.text: So one of the things is people change their-- when they had contact with a gay person discussing gay equality-- they changed their minds, not just about the policy issue about same sex marriage. They also changed their minds about gay people, gays and lesbians as a group.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Nice if that were true. If there were data supporting it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Or there was this finding, which is so particular and specific that again, if there is no data supporting this, it's just a very idiosyncratic thing to decide to say is true. LaCour said that he graded each gay canvasser on how stereotypically gay they appeared. And--

segments.speaker: Michael Lacour
segments.text: The gay canvassers who are perceived as straight had the largest effects.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That is, they were able to convince the most voters to support gay marriage.

segments.speaker: Michael Lacour
segments.text: So this suggests that voters may ordinarily have an unflattering mental image of a stereotypical gay person. And the discrepancy between the stereotype and the person standing on the doorstep creates a space for attitude change.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Right. I see.

segments.speaker: Michael Lacour
segments.text: Especially when the canvassers are building empathy through respectful two-way conversation.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This vision of the world is such a hopeful vision of how the world might work. The world LaCour fabricated is one where intolerant people hold inaccurate stereotypes in their heads and all it takes is an empathetic conversation, one sincere talk, 20 minutes long, with somebody from the stereotyped group and the scales fall from their eyes. They realize they were wrong all along.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I like that world. I wish I lived in that world. Maybe we do live in that world for all we know. But if we do, there's no data proving it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [PHONE RINGING]

segments.speaker: Donald Green
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Hey, Don Green?

segments.speaker: Donald Green
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ira Glass.

segments.speaker: Donald Green
segments.text: Hey, Ira.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Last May, a month after we ran our story about LaCour's study, six months after he published that study in Science magazine, I called his co-author, Columbia professor Donald Green. Green had just reconsidered what was going on in the data LaCour had collected and had asked Science to retract their article, which the magazine did. He seemed understandably sobered and sad.

segments.speaker: Donald Green
segments.text: It was such a waste. Not just of my time, obviously, but no, the Center and the canvassers' time.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Donald Green
segments.text: It's just crazy.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The way the fraud was discovered was actually a little detective story of its own. A detective story that began kind of exactly the way they tell you in school that the scientific method is supposed to work.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Two young researchers-- David Broockman and Joshua Kalla, both in their 20s-- tried to replicate what LaCour did. The  team from the Los Angeles LGBT Center and a Miami LGBT group was organizing a new canvass operation in Miami. Broockman and Kalla would study that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Broockman was already suspicious of LaCour's data. It seemed too perfect. Then they started their research and they noticed something funny.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The way this experiment works, like I said, the researchers do online surveys of the voters' opinions before and after the canvassers come to their doors and talk to them. And the researchers pay the voters to fill out those online surveys to motivate them to do the surveys. And tons of voters filled out LaCour's surveys, but not Broockman and Kalla's.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This made no sense at all. And they didn't know what to do. If people didn't fill out their surveys, they'd have no study. They started to panic.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So they reached out to the survey company that LaCour said he used to find out exactly how LaCour got so many people to fill in their surveys. The company informed them that LaCour was not one of their clients, that the employee LaCour said he worked with did not exist, and in fact, this company did not have the capability to do the things LaCour said they did for him.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The hundreds of thousands of dollars that was supposedly paid out to survey responders, which LaCour said came from funders like the Ford Foundation-- who LaCour thanked in his study-- never was actually granted to LaCour. Given all that, it was hard to see how any of the data could be real.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But LaCour held firm. Said the data was real. He even wrote a paper defending it. But he said that he could not show the data to anybody because he had destroyed all the original surveys to protect the privacy of the respondents.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I'm not sure anybody believed him. He'd been headed for a prestigious job at Princeton University after finishing his doctoral thesis. Now that job evaporated. His collaborator Don Green says the odd thing was the fakery went way beyond what seemed to be necessary.

segments.speaker: Donald Green
segments.text: And this was, I think, the thing that I just want to convey somehow, is that there was an incredible mountain of fabrication. It was the most baroque and ornate ornamentation.

segments.speaker: Donald Green
segments.text: There were stories. There were anecdotes. My Dropbox is filled with graphs and charts.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What do you mean there's stories and anecdotes? I thought the only thing that was fabricated was the online surveys?

segments.speaker: Donald Green
segments.text: Right. But there would be stories out of the survey. So he would say things like, "well did you know that some of the people in the survey came out?"

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: As if, in later surveys, their attitudes about homosexuality had changed enough that they were comfortable finally admitting to the surveyors that they were gay. Except of course, the surveys didn't seem to exist.

segments.speaker: Donald Green
segments.text: It's layer after layer of embellishment that the sheer magnitude of it makes it very hard to entertain the possibility that it's all made up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The day after the truth came to light, one of the guys who created the canvasses, Dave Fleischer, told me that that's what he found himself trying to get his head around, the layers of embellishment. He told me this story about working with Michael LaCour.

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: At our very first canvass where Mike was measuring us, right, we were running the canvass training, we're sending people out canvassing, we're going out canvassing. And Mike has a laptop set up. And as voters that we've talked to then fill out their first post-canvassing survey--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In other words, after real life canvassers came to their doors, Michael LaCour is supposedly having these voters fill out online surveys. And he's telling the canvassers, those surveys--

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: Some of them are starting to trickle in. And Mike's got his laptop set up with him gazing intently at it. And his group of about a half dozen research assistants clustered around him gazing at it raptly, the way you would at election results on a presidential election night.

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: And after we finished the canvass de-brief and the volunteers leave, Mike invites us-- the team of staff organizers-- to come over and also glimpse the findings that are starting to emerge. And I really have thought back on this moment obviously, in the last 24 hours. Because it really looked like, oh my god, the results are coming in.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, wait, wait. And so what was on his screen? Did you see his screen?

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: Oh yeah. It was like a-- heck, it's like data points coming in. And he would go back and forth between these two-- it's probably an old fashioned term from when I studied sociology-- but scattergrams.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: These are like charts.

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: Yes. There's a graphic depiction.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so he's going back and forth. And are those charts changing over the course of the time you look at them?

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's so elaborate.

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: Well, yes. It would have been a whole lot easier just to have measured our work.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: How do you explain this? Like, you worked with him for many, many hours. How are you putting this together in your head?

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: Two years, Ira. And yeah, it is not really understandable to me. Because you spoke, I believe, with Mike on the phone.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Dave Fleischer
segments.text: And he's a smart guy. He, I think, is genuinely a caring guy. He genuinely loves statistics. But there is a piece of this that is incomprehensible when somebody who has so much makes such a grievous choice.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Canvass organizers say staff and 73 volunteers worked for more than 3,600 hours, including knocking on doors and talking to over 400 voters for the fake study. Since all this went down last year, Michael LaCour still has not admitted to fabricating data in public or in private with the colleagues of his that I've spoken to. He declined my invitation to come on the radio this week and talk about this. He declined to say whether the data was real or fake.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The one chink in this position came last month, when out of the blue he texted Dave Fleischer. "Hi Dave. If you're willing, I'd like to meet with you face to face. To apologize." Dave told me he hasn't been able to bring himself to respond just yet. He's not ready.

segments.speaker: David Broockman
segments.text: Yeah, so what we've done so far is the Miami work. I think that's what we're ready to show you some of the early sneak peek into. I think you're the first person outside of the study--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's David Broockman, one of the guys who discovered the fraud in the original study, and the co-author of the new study with real surveys and real data that was published this week in Science magazine. This recording has him talking to me last August, three months after Science retracted the original study.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It was Broockman and his research partner remember, who discovered LaCour's fraud when they tried to replicate his methods in Miami. Now the Miami data was in, the first part of it anyway.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The canvassers in Miami went door to door trying to change voters' attitudes about transgendered people. Miami-Dade County passed an ordinance in 2014 banning discrimination against transgender people. And these canvassers were trying to convince voters that that was a good idea, and to support it if a ballot measure someday tried to strike it down. And they succeeded.

segments.speaker: David Broockman
segments.text: And you see just a huge increase in the acceptance towards transgender people. And overall, what you see is it's basically the largest effect I've ever seen for any political tactic. So much more than phone calls or mail or other forms of canvassing that I've seen. The effect is just huge.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In other words, the thing that was so exciting about the discredited study turned out to be true. These canvasses can change people's minds. For real.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Roughly one out of 10 voters changed their attitudes about transgender people. As the study notes, it took from 1998 to 2012-- 14 years-- for the country as a whole to have a comparable change in its attitudes towards gay people. It only took the canvassers 20 minutes or less to do this for trans people. Broockman said the only political tactic that has ever been shown to be more effective than this in affecting attitudes is personally meeting somebody who's running for office, which of course, is a very different kind of thing.

segments.speaker: David Broockman
segments.text: More impressive is that the effect appears to last, that you basically see the exact same pattern of results six weeks later. We're going to start measuring again at, I think we decided three months and six months. So who knows if these will continue to last into the future?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They did. Three months later, attitudes stayed changed. Again, same as the discredited study.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But where it gets really interesting is the stuff that the new guys found that is different from the original study. First difference? Remember how the original study said that only a gay canvasser could convince a voter to support gay marriage?
